notes.front: What is a ground rod, and what is its primary function?
notes.back: An external earth connection whose primary function is lightning charge dissipation.
notes.explanation: The pool treats “external earth connection” and “ground rod” as the same thing.
notes.example: Like a drain in a courtyard: it gives a sudden flood somewhere to go into the ground.
notes.evidence: What is the primary function of an external earth connection or ground rod? A. Prevent static build up on power lines B. Lightning charge dissipation

notes.front: For an amateur station, who is in an uncontrolled environment for RF exposure purposes?
notes.back: Nearby people who are not members of the licensee’s household; their exposure is judged against the general population/uncontrolled limits.
notes.explanation: Part 97 names these the general population/uncontrolled exposure limits.
notes.example: Like a public footpath beside a building site: passers-by get the stricter protection, not the trained crew.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(c)(1) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: RF exposure of other nearby persons who are not members of the amateur licensee's household must be evaluated with respect to the general population/uncontrolled exposure limits.

notes.front: What is specific absorption rate (SAR)?
notes.back: The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body.
notes.explanation: The pool rejects readings of SAR as a signal attenuation ratio or amplification rating.
notes.example: Like measuring how fast a sponge soaks up water, but for RF energy in body tissue.
notes.evidence: What does SAR measure? A. Signal attenuation ratio B. Signal amplification rating C. The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body

notes.front: In tower safety, what is 100% tie-off?
notes.back: Keeping at least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times.
notes.explanation: The pool rejects tying off ropes, tools or circuit breakers as its meaning.
notes.example: Like crossing a climbing wall on two clip-ins: one stays clipped while you move the other.
notes.evidence: What is meant by “100% tie-off” regarding tower safety? A. All loose ropes and guys secured to a fixed structure B. At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times

notes.front: In tower climbing, what is a lanyard attached to, according to the pool?
notes.back: The tower legs, not the antenna mast, guy brackets or rungs.
notes.explanation: A lanyard is what 100% tie-off keeps attached to the tower at all times.
notes.example: Like a dog’s lead clipped to a fence post rather than to a loose branch.
notes.evidence: To what should lanyards be attached while climbing? A. Antenna mast B. Guy brackets C. Tower rungs D. Tower legs

notes.front: Where does the pool say a shock-absorbing lanyard should be attached when working above ground?
notes.back: To the tower, above the climber’s head level.
notes.explanation: The pool rejects attaching it to the harness belt, at waist level or to the next lowest guys.
notes.example: Like hanging a climbing rope from an anchor overhead rather than at your feet.
notes.evidence: Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground? A. Above the climber’s head level B. To the belt of the fall-arrest harness

notes.front: Against which limits may a licensee evaluate RF exposure of their own household?
notes.back: The occupational/controlled limits, if the licensee and household have accessed appropriate training and information.
notes.explanation: This is an alternative to the general population/uncontrolled limits, open only to the immediate household.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(c)(1) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: In lieu of evaluation with the general population/uncontrolled exposure limits, amateur licensees may evaluate their operation with respect to members of his or her immediate household using the occupational/controlled exposure limits in § 1.1310, provided appropriate training and information has been accessed by the amateur licensee and members of his/her household.

notes.front: If a routine evaluation shows fields could exceed the limits in accessible areas, what must the licensee do?
notes.back: Take action to prevent human exposure to those RF fields.
notes.explanation: The duty applies in accessible areas where the fields could exceed the limits.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(c)(2) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: If the routine environmental evaluation indicates that the RF electromagnetic fields could exceed the limits contained in § 1.1310 of this chapter in accessible areas, the licensee must take action to prevent human exposure to such RF electromagnetic fields.

notes.front: At what available maximum time-averaged power is a single RF source exempt, whatever the separation distance?
notes.back: No more than 1 mW.
notes.explanation: The 1 mW rule applies regardless of how close people are to the source.
notes.evidence: A single RF source is exempt if: (A) The available maximum time-averaged power is no more than 1 mW, regardless of separation distance.

notes.front: An RF exposure exemption relieves a licensee of which obligation only?
notes.back: Performing a routine environmental evaluation to show compliance with the exposure limits.
notes.explanation: It is not exemption from the equipment authorisation procedures of Part 2.
notes.evidence: Exemption for (an) RF source ( s ) is solely from the obligation to perform a routine environmental evaluation to demonstrate compliance with the RF exposure limits in § 1.1310 of this chapter; it is not exemption from the equipment authorization procedures described in part 2 of this chapter,

notes.front: In Table 1 of 1.1307, what threshold ERP applies to a source from 30 to 300 MHz?
notes.back: 3.83 R² watts, where R is the separation distance in metres.
notes.explanation: Unlike the ranges immediately either side (1.34–30 and 300–1,500 MHz), it has no frequency term; it meets them at 30 and 300 MHz, so this is Table 1's lowest threshold.

notes.front: For the Table 1 exemption to apply, how close may the nearby person be at most?
notes.back: No closer than λ/2π, where λ is the free-space operating wavelength in metres.
notes.explanation: R is the minimum separation from the body of a nearby person, and it must be at least λ/2π.
notes.evidence: (C) Or using Table 1 and the minimum separation distance (R in meters) from the body of a nearby person for the frequency (f in MHz) at which the source operates, the ERP (watts) is no more than the calculated value prescribed for that frequency. For the exemption in Table 1 to apply, R must be at least λ/2π,

notes.front: At a multi-transmitter site, field strengths must be {{c1::squared}} to be proportional to SAR or power density.
notes.back: squared
notes.explanation: So the 5% test for a source is applied to the square of its E or H field strength against the square of the limit.
notes.source: 47 CFR 1.1307 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), (b)(5)(i) Multiple fixed RF sources
notes.evidence: Field strengths must be squared to be proportional to SAR or power density. Specifically, these compliance requirements apply if the square of the electric or magnetic field strength exposure level applicable to a particular RF source exceeds 5% of the square of the electric or magnetic field strength limit

notes.front: At a multi-transmitter site over the limits, which licensee has a rebuttable presumption that it should not be liable?
notes.back: One that shows its facility was not the most recently modified or newly constructed at the site.
notes.explanation: The presumption concerns liability in an enforcement proceeding for the period of non-compliance.
notes.source: 47 CFR 1.1307 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), (b)(5)(i) Multiple fixed RF sources
notes.evidence: However, a licensee demonstrating that its facility was not the most recently modified or newly-constructed facility at the site establishes a rebuttable presumption that such licensee should not be liable in an enforcement proceeding relating to the period of non-compliance.

notes.front: On a shared hilltop the total exposure exceeds the limit in one accessible area. Your station produces 3% of its applicable limit there. Are you among those responsible for fixing it?
notes.choices:
A) Yes: every licensee at the site shares the responsibility
B) No: the shared responsibility falls on sources above 5% of their limit there
C) Yes, but only if you run a duty cycle above 50%
D) No: only the site owner is responsible
notes.back: No: the shared responsibility falls on sources above 5% of their limit there
notes.choicesExplained: A: responsibility is shared only by sources above the 5% level. C: the test is the share of the limit, not duty cycle. D: the rule places the responsibility on licensees.
notes.explanation: The rule assigns the fix to licensees whose sources exceed 5% of the applicable limit at that area.
notes.source: 47 CFR 1.1307 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), (b)(5)(i) Multiple fixed RF sources
notes.evidence: are the shared responsibility of all licensees whose RF sources produce, at the area in question, levels that exceed 5% of the applicable exposure limit proportional to power.

notes.front: Climbing past a guy bracket, you must unclip a lanyard. How do you keep 100% tie-off?
notes.back: Clip a second lanyard to the tower first, then release the first one.
notes.explanation: At least one lanyard must stay attached to the tower at all times, so you are never unclipped.
notes.evidence: B. At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times

notes.front: A sensor transmitter has an available maximum time-averaged power of 0.5 mW and sits close to users. Is it exempt from routine RF exposure evaluation?
notes.back: Yes: a single source of no more than 1 mW is exempt regardless of separation distance.
notes.explanation: The distance to users does not matter under this exemption.
notes.evidence: A single RF source is exempt if: (A) The available maximum time-averaged power is no more than 1 mW, regardless of separation distance.

notes.front: Your trained household versus your next-door neighbour: which RF exposure limits may apply to each?
notes.back: Household, with training and information accessed: occupational/controlled limits. Neighbour: general population/uncontrolled limits.
notes.explanation: The controlled limits are allowed only in lieu of the uncontrolled ones, and only for the immediate household.
notes.source: 47 CFR Part 97 (rev. 1 Oct 2025), § 97.13(c)(1) Restrictions on station location
notes.evidence: In lieu of evaluation with the general population/uncontrolled exposure limits, amateur licensees may evaluate their operation with respect to members of his or her immediate household using the occupational/controlled exposure limits in § 1.1310, provided appropriate training and information has been accessed by the amateur licensee and members of his/her household.

notes.front: Lanyards while climbing versus a shock-absorbing lanyard when working above ground: where does the pool attach each?
notes.back: Lanyards while climbing: the tower legs. Shock-absorbing lanyard at work: above the climber’s head level.
notes.explanation: The pool keys the tower legs for climbing and a point above head level for a shock-absorbing lanyard.
notes.evidence: To what should lanyards be attached while climbing? A. Antenna mast B. Guy brackets C. Tower rungs D. Tower legs ~~ E0A12 (A) Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground? A. Above the climber’s head level

notes.front: What is the primary function of an external earth connection or ground rod?
notes.choices:
A) Prevent static build up on power lines
B) Lightning charge dissipation
C) Reduce RF current flow between pieces of equipment
D) Protect breaker panel from power surges
notes.back: Lightning charge dissipation
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: static on power lines, RF currents between pieces of equipment and surges at the breaker panel are handled by other means, such as bonding and surge protection.
notes.explanation: A lightning strike brings a huge charge in an instant; an external earth connection gives it a short, low-resistance path into the ground outside the house.
notes.evidence:
E0A01 (B)
What is the primary function of an external earth connection or ground rod?
A. Prevent static build up on power lines
B. Lightning charge dissipation
C. Reduce RF current flow between pieces of equipment
D. Protect breaker panel from power surges

notes.front: When evaluating RF exposure levels from your station at a neighbor’s home, what must you do?
notes.choices:
A) Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
B) Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
C) Ensure signals from your station are less than the controlled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits
D) Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible emission (MPE) limits
notes.back: Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible exposure (MPE) limits
notes.choicesExplained: A: controlled limits are allowed only for the trained household. C and D: MPE stands for maximum permissible exposure, not emission.
notes.explanation: Part 97 says people outside the licensee’s household must be evaluated against the general population/uncontrolled exposure limits (97.13(c)(1)).
notes.evidence:
B. Ensure signals from your station are less than the uncontrolled maximum permissible exposure (MPE)
limits

notes.front: Over what range of frequencies are the FCC human body RF exposure limits most restrictive?
notes.choices:
A) 300 kHz - 3 MHz
B) 3 - 30 MHz
C) 30 - 300 MHz
D) 300 - 3000 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D: Table 1 of 1.1307 allows more power before an evaluation in these ranges, so the limits there are less restrictive.
notes.explanation: Table 1 of 1.1307 shows the same pattern: the ERP that triggers an evaluation is lowest, a flat 3.83 R² watts, across 30–300 MHz, and higher on either side.
notes.evidence:
E0A03 (C)
Over what range of frequencies are the FCC human body RF exposure limits most restrictive?
A. 300 kHz - 3 MHz
B. 3 - 30 MHz
C. 30 - 300 MHz
D. 300 - 3000 MHz

notes.front: When evaluating a site with multiple transmitters operating at the same time, the operators and licensees of which transmitters are responsible for mitigating over-exposure situations?
notes.choices:
A) Each transmitter that produces 20 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
B) Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 25 percent
C) Each transmitter that produces 5 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
D) Each transmitter operating with a duty cycle greater than 50 percent
notes.back: Each transmitter that produces 5 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit is exceeded
notes.choicesExplained: A: 20% is not the figure. B and D: the test is each source’s share of the limit, not its duty cycle.
notes.explanation: Section 1.1307(b) makes the fix the shared responsibility of licensees whose sources produce more than 5% of the applicable limit at the area in question.
notes.evidence:
C. Each transmitter that produces 5 percent or more of its MPE limit in areas where the total MPE limit
is exceeded

notes.front: What hazard is created by operating at microwave frequencies?
notes.choices:
A) Microwaves are ionizing radiation
B) The high gain antennas commonly used can result in high exposure levels
C) Microwaves are in the frequency range where wave velocity is higher
D) The extremely high frequency energy can damage the joints of antenna structures
notes.back: The high gain antennas commonly used can result in high exposure levels
notes.choicesExplained: A: microwaves are non-ionizing radiation; their hazard is heating. C: all radio waves travel at the same speed in free space. D: RF energy does not damage the joints of antenna structures.
notes.explanation: A high-gain antenna such as a dish concentrates the transmitter's power into a narrow beam, so the power density in front of it can be high even at modest power.
notes.evidence: B. The high gain antennas commonly used can result in high exposure levels

notes.front: Why are there separate electric (E) and magnetic (H) MPE limits at frequencies below 300 MHz?
notes.choices:
A) The body reacts to electromagnetic radiation from both the E and H fields
B) Ground reflections and scattering cause the field strength to vary with location
C) E field and H field radiation intensity peaks can occur at different locations
D) All these choices are correct
notes.back: All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each is one of the reasons, so D, which includes all three, is keyed.
notes.explanation: The pool gives three reasons: the body reacts to both fields, reflections and scattering make field strength vary with place, and E and H peaks can fall in different places.
notes.evidence:
E0A06 (D)
Why are there separate electric (E) and magnetic (H) MPE limits at frequencies below 300 MHz?
A. The body reacts to electromagnetic radiation from both the E and H fields
B. Ground reflections and scattering cause the field strength to vary with location
C. E field and H field radiation intensity peaks can occur at different locations

notes.front: What is meant by “100% tie-off” regarding tower safety?
notes.choices:
A) All loose ropes and guys secured to a fixed structure
B) At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times
C) All tools secured to the climber’s harness
D) All circuit breakers feeding power to the tower must be tied closed with tape, cable, or ties
notes.back: At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D: securing ropes, tools or circuit breakers is not what the term means.
notes.explanation: With at least one lanyard attached at all times, a climber is never unprotected, even while moving the other lanyard past an obstacle.
notes.evidence: B. At least one lanyard attached to the tower at all times

notes.front: What does SAR measure?
notes.choices:
A) Signal attenuation ratio
B) Signal amplification rating
C) The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body
D) The rate of RF energy reflected from stationary terrain
notes.back: The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: SAR is not a signal ratio or rating. D: it measures absorption by the body, not reflection from terrain.
notes.explanation: SAR is the specific absorption rate: the rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body.
notes.evidence: C. The rate at which RF energy is absorbed by the body

notes.front: Which of the following types of equipment are exempt from RF exposure evaluations?
notes.choices:
A) Transceivers with less than 7 watts of RF output
B) Antennas that radiate only in the near field
C) Hand-held transceivers sold before May 3, 2021
D) Dish antennas less than one meter in diameter
notes.back: Hand-held transceivers sold before May 3, 2021
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 1.1307 single-source power exemption is 1 mW, not 7 W. B and D: 1.1307 gives no exemption for near-field antennas or small dishes.
notes.explanation: 3 May 2021 is when the FCC's revised RF exposure rules took effect. The FCC's notice lets certified equipment keep relying on compliance with the earlier rules unless it is modified, and the pool keys hand-helds sold before that date as exempt.
notes.evidence: C. Hand-held transceivers sold before May 3, 2021

notes.front: When must an RF exposure evaluation be performed on an amateur station operating on 80 meters?
notes.choices:
A) An evaluation must always be performed
B) When the ERP of the station is less than 10 watts
C) When the station’s operating mode is CW
D) When the output power from the transmitter is less than 100 watts
notes.back: An evaluation must always be performed
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: 1.1307 offers none of these as a way out; its exemptions depend on power, frequency and distance together, and checking them is part of the assessment.
notes.explanation: Under 1.1307(b)(1) a licensee must either show that the station qualifies for an exemption under 1.1307(b)(3) or prepare an evaluation, so an 80 m station is always assessed.
notes.evidence: A. An evaluation must always be performed

notes.front: To what should lanyards be attached while climbing?
notes.choices:
A) Antenna mast
B) Guy brackets
C) Tower rungs
D) Tower legs
notes.back: Tower legs
notes.choicesExplained: A: a mast is a separate pipe that can slip or bend. B: guy brackets are made to hold guy wires, not a falling climber. C: rungs are lighter cross-members, not the main structure.
notes.explanation: The legs are the tower's main load-bearing members, fixed to its base, so they can hold the force of a fall.
notes.evidence:
E0A11 (D)
To what should lanyards be attached while climbing?
A. Antenna mast
B. Guy brackets
C. Tower rungs
D. Tower legs

notes.front: Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground?
notes.choices:
A) Above the climber’s head level
B) To the belt of the fall-arrest harness
C) Even with the climber's waist
D) To the next lowest set of guys
notes.back: Above the climber’s head level
notes.choicesExplained: B and C: a lanyard at belt or waist level lets the climber fall its full length before it catches. D: the next lowest guys are below the climber, so the fall would be longer still.
notes.explanation: Attached above head level, the lanyard leaves little slack, so a fall is short and the shock absorber can stop it before the climber drops far.
notes.evidence:
E0A12 (A)
Where should a shock-absorbing lanyard be attached to a tower when working above ground?
A. Above the climber’s head level
B. To the belt of the fall-arrest harness
C. Even with the climber's waist
D. To the next lowest set of guys
